title: What's this, who's that
title_target: ეს რა არის? — Es ra aris?
goal: Point at things and people around you, ask what something is called in Georgian, answer yes and no, and form plurals with one ending that works for every word.
bekal: ask ეს რა არის? and ის ვინ არის?
use კი, დიახ, არა, and არ each in the right place
make any noun plural with the ending -ები

dialogs.title: დიალოგი — In the classroom
dialogs.intro: Lesson two. Giorgi, the teacher, points at things around the room and Ani names them. Notice how the verb "is" sticks to the end of the noun — in this whole dialogue there's hardly a single არის standing on its own.

lines.speaker: ანი:
lines.id: It's a pen… no, a pencil.

lines.speaker: ანი:
lines.id: That's a table. There are books on the table.

lines.speaker: ანი:
lines.id: I don't know. What is it in Georgian?

lines.speaker: ანი:
lines.id: Panjara. This is a door, right?

lines.speaker: გიორგი:
lines.id: Yes, it's a door. Well done, Ani!

notes: **ეს = this (near), ის = that (far).** ⚠️ Notice that **ის also means "he/she"** — exactly the same word. *ის ვინ არის?* can mean "who's that?" or "who is he/she?", and only the situation decides: if you're pointing, it means "that". Georgian doesn't feel the need to separate people from things here.

**"Is" sticks on as -ა or -ია.** Nouns ending in **-ი** drop the -ი and add **-ია**: წიგნ**ი** → წიგნ**ია**, კარ**ი** → კარ**ია**. Nouns ending in **-ა** just add **-ა**: მაგიდა → მაგიდა**ა** (said with a slightly long a), ფანჯარა → ფანჯარა**ა**. The long form (წიგნი არის) isn't wrong, but it sounds like reading out a list.

**არ and არა are two different words.** ⚠️ A classic trap: English has "no" and "not", and Georgian splits them the same way. **არა** = "no" standing alone, as an answer to a question. **არ** = "not", placed **before the verb**: არ ვიცი (I don't know), არ არის (isn't / there isn't). Never answer a question with არ on its own.

**ვიცი means "I know", and it doesn't take the usual ვ- prefix.** It's one of a handful of very common irregular verbs: ვიცი (I know), იცი (you know), იცის (he/she knows). Learn all three now; you'll use them every day.

**ქართულად როგორ არის? — learn this sentence as a whole.** It means "what is it in Georgian?", and it lets you grow your vocabulary without a dictionary, straight from the person in front of you. The ending **-ად** in ქართულ**ად** means "in / -ly" and is covered fully in the next unit.

**რამდენი წიგნია? — the noun stays singular.** ⚠️ After a number or "how many", Georgian nouns are **not** made plural: სამი წიგნი (three book), ათი ლარი (ten lari). Unlike English, it's "three book" — a relief, not a trap. What's actually wrong is სამი წიგნები.
**ყოჩაღ!** (q'ochagh) — everyday praise meaning roughly "well done, nice work". Teachers say it to students, parents to children, friends to friends. If you hear it, you're doing something right.

grammars.title: Plurals: one ending for every word, no exceptions
body: After wrestling with English plurals (child/children, mouse/mice) or Russian ones, this part feels like a gift. Georgian makes the plural with **-ები** for any word, with not a single irregular form.
after: There's only one rule: **the final vowel drops first**, then -ები is added. წიგნ**ი** → წიგნ**ები**, მაგიდ**ა** → მაგიდ**ები**.

⚠️ But remember the note above: **no plural after numbers**. The plural is used when the number isn't stated — *მაგიდაზე წიგნებია* (there are books on the table), but *მაგიდაზე სამი წიგნია* (there are three books on the table).

grammars.title: Yes, no, and not
body: Georgian has three ways to say "yes" at different levels of politeness, and picking the wrong one is harmless — it just sounds too casual or too stiff.

an answer standing on its own

after: One habit that confuses foreigners: answering negative questions. If someone asks *ჩაი არ გინდა?* (don't you want tea?), the answer **კი** means "right, I don't" to some people and "yes, I do!" to others. To be safe, don't answer with one word: say **კი, მინდა** or **არა, არ მინდა**.

blocks.text: The fastest way to build vocabulary in week one isn't memorizing lists but naming the things actually in front of you. Read the left-hand column while pointing at each object.

blocks.title: Four sentences for any classroom
items: **ეს ქართულად როგორ არის?** — What is this in Georgian?
**გაიმეორეთ, თუ შეიძლება.** (gaimeoret, tu sheidzleba) — Please repeat.
**ნელა, თუ შეიძლება.** (nela, tu sheidzleba) — Slowly, please.
**როგორ იწერება?** (rogor its'ereba) — How do you write it?

blocks.text: Notice **თუ შეიძლება** (tu sheidzleba) — literally "if it's possible", and this is the Georgian "please". Like English *please*, it usually goes at the end of the sentence. You'll use it for the rest of this course, especially when ordering at the café in unit 5.
